findings.title: Google credential key is overwritten with the zod SafeParse wrapper object instead of the token data
findings.body: `parseRefreshTokenResponse()` returns the raw `safeParse` result (`{ success: true, data: {...} }`), not the parsed token. The Google refresh path does `const key = parseRefreshTokenResponse(googleCredentials, googleCredentialSchema)` and then `prisma.credential.update({ data: { key } })`, so the stored `credential.key` becomes `{ success: true, data: { access_token, ... } }`. The next time a `GoogleCalendarService` is constructed, `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)` throws because the required fields now live under `.data`, so Google Calendar stops working for every user after their first token refresh, regardless of whether credential sync is enabled. Previously `googleCredentialSchema.parse(googleCredentials)` returned the data directly. Use `.data` (as the Office365/Zoom/Salesforce callers do) or make the helper return the parsed data.

findings.title: `prisma` is used but never imported in the Salesforce CalendarService
findings.body: The new code in `getClient` calls `prisma.credential.update(...)` at line 96, but this file has no `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"` (the import list only contains jsforce, rrule, zod, CalEventParser, constants, http-error, logger, types, getAppKeysFromSlug and parseRefreshTokenResponse). This fails type-check and, at runtime, throws `ReferenceError: prisma is not defined` on every Salesforce service instantiation, breaking the Salesforce integration completely.

findings.title: Salesforce now refreshes the token on every service instantiation and then ignores the new access token
findings.body: `getClient` is invoked from the constructor and now unconditionally POSTs to `https://login.salesforce.com/services/oauth2/token` with `grant_type=refresh_token` on every instantiation, with no expiry check. This adds a network round trip and a DB write to every booking/availability call and burns through Salesforce's refresh rate limits. Worse, after writing the refreshed token to the DB, the `jsforce.Connection` is still created with `credentialKey.access_token` / `credentialKey.instance_url` (the OLD values from `credential.key`), so the freshly obtained access token is never used. Also, unlike every other app in this PR, this path does not go through `refreshOAuthTokens`, so credential sync is silently not applied to Salesforce. Additionally `response.statusText !== "OK"` is unreliable (statusText is empty under HTTP/2); check `response.ok` instead.

findings.title: Zoho Bigin passes `credentialId` where `refreshOAuthTokens` expects `userId`
findings.body: `refreshOAuthTokens(fn, "zoho-bigin", credentialId)` passes the credential's primary key as the third argument, but the helper's signature is `(refreshFunction, appSlug, userId: number | null)` and it sends that value as `calcomUserId` to `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT`. With credential sync enabled, the self-hoster's endpoint will be asked for the tokens of whatever user happens to have `id === credentialId`, and those tokens are then written into this credential and used for API calls — a cross-user credential leak. `refreshAccessToken` only receives `credentialId` and `credentialKey`; it needs `credential.userId` threaded through (as every other app does).

findings.title: `minimumTokenResponseSchema` uses bogus computed keys and strips every field except `access_token`
findings.body: `[z.string().toString()]: z.number()` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]: z.unknown().optional()` do not create pattern/catch-all keys; `ZodType.toString()` returns `"[object Object]"`, so both lines define the same literal property `"[object Object]"` (the second overrides the first). The resulting schema is effectively `z.object({ access_token: z.string() })`, and since `z.object` strips unknown keys by default, when `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED && CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` is set the returned `data` contains only `access_token`. Consequences: Office365 loses `expires_in`/`expiry` (so `isExpired` sees undefined and refreshes on every call), Zoom computes `expiry_date = Date.now() + undefined * 1000 = NaN` (serialized to `null` in JSON, after which `zoomTokenSchema.parse` fails forever with "Zoom credential keys parsing error"), and Salesforce loses `instance_url`. The comment "Assume that any property with a number is the expiry" is not implemented. Use `.passthrough()` or `z.record()`/`.catchall()` and validate the expiry explicitly.

findings.title: Injecting the literal string "refresh_token" clobbers real refresh tokens in the DB
findings.body: When the parsed response lacks `refresh_token`, the helper sets `data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"` (a placeholder string). Callers then persist this: Zoom does `key.refresh_token = newTokens.refresh_token` and Office365 does `{ ...o365AuthCredentials, ...tokenResponse.data }`, so the user's genuine refresh token in `credential.key` is overwritten with the literal `"refresh_token"`. This happens in sync mode for Zoom (the minimum schema never includes refresh_token) and in normal mode for Office365 whenever Microsoft omits `refresh_token` from a refresh response (the schema marks it optional). Previously zod omitted absent optional keys so the spread preserved the stored value. Once clobbered, disabling sync (or the next normal refresh) fails permanently with invalid_grant and the user must reconnect the app. Don't mutate the parsed data; leave the field absent and let callers keep the existing stored refresh token.

findings.title: Sync branch returns a raw fetch `Response` but several callers expect an axios response or an already-parsed token object
findings.body: In the sync branch `refreshOAuthTokens` returns the `fetch` `Response` object, whereas the per-app `refreshFunction`s return heterogeneous shapes that the callers depend on: Google returns a gaxios response and reads `res.data.access_token`; HubSpot returns a parsed `HubspotToken` and reads `.accessToken`/`.expiresIn`; Zoho CRM and Zoho Bigin return an axios response and read `.data.error`/`.data.access_token`. With sync enabled, Google hits `token.access_token` on `undefined` (TypeError, swallowed by the catch and the expired token is reused), Zoho CRM/Bigin throw `Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'error')`, and HubSpot stores a mangled object with `expiryDate: NaN` and `accessToken: undefined`. Only the apps whose refresh functions already return a `fetch` `Response` (Lark, Office365, Webex, Zoom, MS Teams) work. The helper must normalize the sync response (e.g. `await response.json()`) into the shape each caller expects, or callers must branch on sync mode.

findings.title: Request to CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT carries no authentication
findings.body: The sync request POSTs only `calcomUserId` and `appSlug` as form fields with no shared secret, signature or bearer header. The self-hoster's endpoint therefore has no way to verify the request came from Cal.com, and anyone who can reach that endpoint can obtain any user's third-party access tokens simply by posting a user id. The inbound webhook (`app-credential.ts`) uses `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`; the outbound request should at minimum send that secret in `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME` so the endpoint can authenticate the caller. The comment "Customize the payload based on what your endpoint requires" also implies self-hosters are expected to edit source, which is not a viable contract. Note also the `appSlug` values are inconsistent: Zoom passes `"zoomvideo"` (directory name) while its DB slug is `"zoom"`, and MS Teams passes `"msteams"` (slug).

findings.title: `appStoreMetadata` is keyed by app directory name, not by App.slug, so most apps return 404
findings.body: The handler looks up the app by `prisma.app.findUnique({ where: { slug } })` and then indexes `appStoreMetadata[app.slug]`. `appStoreMetadata` (from `@calcom/app-store/appStoreMetaData`, built from `apps.metadata.generated.ts`) is keyed by directory name — `googlecalendar`, `zoomvideo`, `office365calendar`, `larkcalendar`, `office365video` — while the DB slugs are `google-calendar`, `zoom`, `office365-calendar`, `lark-calendar`, `msteams`. For all of those the lookup yields `undefined` and the webhook responds `404 "App not found. Ensure that you have the correct app slug"`, so the headline feature cannot sync credentials for the main calendar/video apps. Only apps whose dirName equals their slug (hubspot, salesforce, zohocrm, webex, zoho-bigin) happen to work. Look the metadata up by matching `.slug` (e.g. `Object.values(appStoreMetadata).find(m => m.slug === app.slug)`) or use the `type`/`dirName` stored on the App row.

findings.title: Webhook secret compared with `!==` and endpoint accepts any HTTP method
findings.body: The shared secret is compared with a plain string `!==`, which is not constant-time; use `crypto.timingSafeEqual` on equal-length buffers. The handler also does not restrict `req.method` to POST, and `req.headers[...]` may be a `string[]` if the header is repeated. Additionally, if `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` were ever unset the `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED` check happens to protect it, but the comparison itself would otherwise be `undefined !== undefined === false` and allow unauthenticated writes — worth an explicit guard.

findings.title: Schema `.parse`, `symmetricDecrypt` and `JSON.parse` failures surface as unhandled 500s
findings.body: `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` throws a `ZodError` on invalid input, and `symmetricDecrypt(...)` / `JSON.parse(...)` throw on a bad key or malformed ciphertext. None of these are caught and the handler is not wrapped in `defaultResponder`, so callers get a generic 500 with a stack trace instead of a 400 with a useful message, and the server logs noise for every malformed webhook. Use `safeParse` and a try/catch around decryption, returning 400.

findings.title: No tests for the new webhook endpoint or the shared OAuth helpers
findings.body: The PR adds a new authenticated API route that writes third-party credentials into the database, plus two helpers (`refreshOAuthTokens`, `parseRefreshTokenResponse`) that are now on the token-refresh path of 10+ integrations, with zero automated tests (the author's checklist confirms this). Several of the defects in this PR — the Google key being stored as a SafeParse wrapper, the broken computed-key zod schema, the missing `prisma` import in Salesforce, the dirName-vs-slug metadata lookup — would have been caught by even a minimal unit test of each helper and a request-level test of the webhook. At minimum add tests for: secret validation, 404 paths, create-vs-update, and `parseRefreshTokenResponse` output in both sync and non-sync modes.
